newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to grant amnesty over 1947 massacre.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to grant amnesty over 1947 massacre.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui plans to grant amnesty to people accused of anti-government activities during a 1947 massacre that killed 18,000 people, an official said on Tuesday.

A spokesman for Lee's office said the president had approved the cabinet's suggestion to issue the Nationalist government's first mass amnesty since it retreated to Taiwan from mainland China in 1949.
"The president has approved the suggestion, and has asked the justice ministry to work out the wording and other details of the amnesty," the spokesman told Reuters.
"This is an important step for historic reconciliation," he said.

The amnesty would apply to anyone -- living or dead -- who was accused of anti-government activities in connection with the 1947 massacre universally known in Taiwan simply as "2-28", a reference to the date when it began, February 28.
It was on that date that Nationalist troops fleeing China's communist takeover began gunning down Taiwan civilians to assert their authority in the face of perceived political resistance.
Until martial law finally was lifted in 1987, 2-28 was a political taboo that was never mentioned in public.

Despite a political renaissance that began in the late 1980s, the Nationalists did not address the massacre until February 1995, when Lee, Taiwan's first native-born president, made the government's first official apology.
In March 1995, parliament approved granting up to T$6 million (US$218,000) to each survivor of known victims.
Today, with democracy in full bloom, Taiwan is taking quickening steps towards a full public reconciliation.
February 28 was marked for the first time in 1997 as an official holiday, proclaimed a few days earlier by parliament.
The Nationalists took control of Taiwan after Japan's World War Two defeat in 1945 ended Tokyo's 50-year occupation of the island.

The massacre, sparked by an elderly woman's protest against the expropriation of untaxed cigarettes, came as Nationalist troops moved to secure Taiwan in their losing battle against a communist takeover of the mainland.
